title: Introduction: Methods, Sources, Aims of Legal History

2.title: Who teaches the course
2.text: Six teachers share the lecture, and the division matters for the exam: the topic list tells you whose chapter you are in. Olechowski takes the introduction, antiquity, the Middle Ages, the ius commune, the Austrian First Republic and European integration; Foljanty the common law, the Westphalian order, natural law and revolutions, legal professions, imperialism and globalization; Staudigl-Ciechowicz constitutionalism and norm production, the dictatorships and the Cold War; Wendehorst Jewish legal history; Li Chinese legal history; Gassner the First World War and the peace treaties.

3.title: The schedule is the exam's table of contents
3.text: Twenty-four sessions, twenty-four exam topics, in this order: introduction and method; ancient legal cultures and Islamic law; the Middle Ages; the ius commune and early modern times; Jewish legal history; the common law; the Westphalian order and early constitutionalism; natural law, Enlightenment and revolutions; constitutionalism and norm production I–III; legal education and the legal professions; imperialism before 1914; Chinese legal history; the First World War and the Paris peace conference; the Austrian First Republic and the B-VG I–II; the dictatorships of the twentieth century I–II; Europe in the Cold War 1945–1955; European integration since 1955; Her Story; the globalization of law I–II. The same list, with the required reading against each item, is the handout 'What to read for the exam'.

cards.q: How is the material of this course divided, and where do you find the authoritative list?
cards.a: Into 24 topics, one per session, running chronologically from method and antiquity to the globalization of law. The authoritative list — topic by topic, with the required reading for each — is the handout 'What to read for the exam' (Modulprüfung).

4.title: Where the material lives
4.text: Moodle for the slides and the article PDFs, rechtsgeschichte.univie.ac.at for the department.

5.title: The exam: format and terms
5.text: The lecture is a compulsory subject of the curriculum and is held in the winter semester only. The module examination is WRITTEN and lasts 120 minutes, with several terms a year — January 26, March 3, May 5, June 24 in the cycle shown on the slide. Registration periods are separate for each term and are easy to miss. The questions are of two kinds: questions testing knowledge and comprehension, and sources — an excerpt you are asked to place, explain and connect.

cards.q: What is the format of the module examination, and what two kinds of question does it contain?
cards.a: A written exam of 120 minutes, offered at several terms a year (January, March, May, June). It asks questions of knowledge and comprehension, and source questions — an excerpt to be placed, explained and connected to the wider development.

6.title: The practical exercises
6.text: The Praktische Übung is not required by the curriculum but is strongly recommended: it goes through source texts together and its short tests are written in the same way as the exam. That is where the 'Questions and Sources' handouts come from, and they are the closest thing to a list of what will actually be asked.

7.title: What will be tested
7.text: Three things, and the slides are only one of them: the content presented orally in the lecture (the slides support it, they do not replace it); the textbook Th. Olechowski, Introduction to Austrian and European Legal History, 2nd ed., Vienna 2025; and fourteen articles on special topics, available as PDFs on Moodle. The reading list ties each article to the topic it belongs to.

cards.q: What three bodies of material does the module examination cover?
cards.a: The content presented orally in the lecture (slides only support it), the textbook Olechowski, Introduction to Austrian and European Legal History (2nd ed. 2025), and the fourteen articles on special topics posted on Moodle.

9.title: Why legal history?
9.text: The honest opening question: is 'education as a value in itself' enough to justify making legal history compulsory in the first year? The slide sets up a second question to answer the first — to which family does legal history belong: to the history of medicine and physics, or to the history of philosophy and the arts? The point is that it belongs cleanly to neither. Legal history is written between a historical interest (what happened) and a legal interest (what the law was and what it did), and the whole method follows from that double position.

terms.term: legal history between historical and legal interest
terms.def: The discipline's double position: it reconstructs the past like history, but its object is a normative order, so it must also ask what counted as valid law at the time. Neither purely a historical nor purely a doctrinal subject.

cards.q: Between which two interests does legal history sit, and why does that placement decide its method?
cards.a: Between a historical interest (who, where, when, what, why) and a legal interest (was the act lawful under the law then in force). Because its object is a normative order, it must reconstruct the legal ideas of contemporaries, not apply today's law to the past.

cards.q: Give three reasons why legal history is useful to a lawyer.
cards.a: It shows today's complicated law emerging from its simplest elements, so the structure of current law becomes intelligible (Mitteis). It exposes the forces that drive legal change, so a lawyer can read the law as something made rather than given. And it destroys the assumption of automatic progress, showing that any legal order can relapse (Ogris).

10.title: What is law? The question itself
10.text: People have dealt with law for millennia without ever agreeing on what law is in the first place. The slide is deliberately deflationary: the course does not open with a definition handed down as settled, but with the fact that the definition is contested — which is why the next slides give two rival answers before the lecturer gives his own.

11.title: Natural law against legal positivism
11.text: The two classic answers, each named after a representative. Samuel Pufendorf (1632–1694) stands for NATURAL LAW, the law of reason: there is an idea of a legal and just order derived purely from reason, therefore unchangeable by humans and valid in the same way everywhere on earth. Hans Kelsen (1881–1973) stands for LEGAL POSITIVISM: law is made by humans alone, and for that very reason it can have 'any content whatsoever'. The consequence is the one that matters for the rest of the course — on the positivist view an unjust rule is still law, and the question of whether it is just is a separate question.

terms.def: The view that a just legal order can be derived from reason itself, is therefore not at the disposal of human legislators, and holds everywhere alike. Pufendorf is the representative here.
The view that law is made by humans alone and can therefore have any content whatsoever; validity and justice are separate questions. Kelsen is the representative here.

cards.q: What separates natural law from legal positivism on the question of what law can contain?
cards.a: Natural law derives a just order from reason, so it is unchangeable by humans and the same everywhere — content is limited in advance. Legal positivism holds that law is made by humans alone and can therefore have 'any content whatsoever'; whether it is just is a separate question.

cards.q: Who is named for natural law and who for legal positivism in this lecture, and when did they live?
cards.a: Samuel Pufendorf (1632–1694) for natural law / the law of reason; Hans Kelsen (1881–1973) for legal positivism.

12.title: Four pictures, one problem
12.text: The slide sets four images beside one another: the Nazi Volksgerichtshof, the court for political trials; Eleanor Roosevelt with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights drafted under her leadership; the Crusades; and the Taliban in Afghanistan. They are not there to be ranked. They make the positivist point visible: each of these orders was, in its own time and place, generally effective and applied organized coercion, and each would have described itself as law. If law were defined by justice, most of what legal history studies would not be law at all — and the discipline could not do its work.

cards.q: Why does the lecture put the Nazi People's Court, the UDHR, the Crusades and the Taliban on one slide?
cards.a: To show that a definition of law cannot be built out of justice. Each was an effective order applying organized coercion and understood itself as law. Legal history has to be able to study orders it rejects, so validity and justice are kept apart.

13.title: European legal culture
13.text: European legal culture is the product of thousands of years of development, and its peculiarities only become fully apparent when that development is examined and compared with other legal cultures. This is the justification for the word 'global' in the course title: the Jewish, Islamic and Chinese chapters are not decoration, they are the comparison that makes the European material legible as one possibility among several.

cards.q: What is the argument for teaching European legal history GLOBALLY rather than on its own?
cards.a: The peculiarities of European legal culture only become visible in comparison. Treated alone it looks like the natural shape of law; set beside Jewish, Islamic and Chinese law it appears as one long development among several possible ones.

14.title: The purpose of legal history: Mitteis and Ogris
14.text: Two quotations set the aims. Heinrich Mitteis (1889–1952): legal history 'introduces us to the modern law by allowing its complicated structure to emerge from its simplest basic elements; it exposes the driving forces that lead to the development of law as the life-conditioning order of every community.' Werner Ogris (1935–2015) adds the corrective: legal history 'must resolutely counter the delusion that the development of a legal order will always lead, almost automatically, to a higher degree of perfection. The opposite is the case: no era and no legal order is free of challenges and the risk of relapse.' Mitteis gives the constructive aim, Ogris the critical one — and the twentieth-century chapters of this course are Ogris's argument in detail.

cards.q: What does Mitteis say legal history does for the understanding of modern law?
cards.a: It lets the complicated structure of modern law emerge from its simplest basic elements, and exposes the driving forces behind legal development — law being the life-conditioning order of every community.

cards.q: What delusion does Ogris say legal history must counter?
cards.a: That a legal order develops almost automatically towards ever greater perfection. No era and no legal order is free of challenges and of the risk of relapse — progress is not guaranteed.

15.title: The definition used in this course
15.text: The lecturer's own answer, and that of the Vienna School of Legal Theory: 'Law is a regulatory system which is created by humans for humans and is generally effective, and which may apply organized coercion.' Take the elements apart, because the exam does. Created by humans FOR humans — so it is positive law, and it regulates human conduct. GENERALLY EFFECTIVE — not obeyed in every case, but by and large in force; an order nobody follows any more has ceased to be law. MAY apply organized coercion — the coercion is organized (not private force) and it is a possibility, not a requirement in every norm.

terms.def: A regulatory system created by humans for humans, generally effective, which may apply organized coercion. The definition of the Vienna School of Legal Theory.
By and large in force in a community — not obeyed in every single case, but not a dead letter either. The criterion that distinguishes law in force from a rule that has lapsed.

cards.q: Give the definition of law used in this course, and name its elements.
cards.a: 'Law is a regulatory system which is created by humans for humans and is generally effective, and which may apply organized coercion.' Elements: created by humans (positive law), for humans (it regulates human conduct), general effectiveness (by and large in force), and the possibility of organized — not private — coercion.

cards.q: Why does the definition say law MAY apply organized coercion rather than must?
cards.a: Because coercion is a possibility the order holds in reserve, not a feature of every single norm; many rules are followed without it. What matters is that the coercion available is organized by the order itself rather than left to private force.

16.title: What is the state?
16.text: The state of the modern age is a relatively centralised legal order with a relatively precisely defined personal scope (the state people) and spatial scope (the state territory). Both qualifications carry weight: 'relatively' centralised and 'relatively' precisely defined. States in older times have little in common with this modern concept — the slide sets the Austrian National Council against the Imperial Diet at Worms in 1495 to make the gap visible. Reading modern statehood back into the Middle Ages is the standard beginner's error in this subject.

terms.def: A relatively centralised legal order with a relatively precisely defined personal scope (state people) and spatial scope (state territory).

cards.q: How does this course define the modern state, and what warning goes with the definition?
cards.a: A relatively centralised legal order with a relatively precisely defined personal scope (state people) and spatial scope (state territory). The warning: older political formations have little in common with it — the Imperial Diet at Worms in 1495 is not an early parliament of a state in this sense.

17.title: State law and international law (1)
17.text: The diagram places the international community above the individual states: international law governs the relations BETWEEN the legal orders, while each state law governs within its own scope. The two are drawn as different levels, not as competitors on the same plane.

18.title: State law and international law (2)
18.text: The same picture with two state legal orders side by side under one international law. The structural point: state law is hierarchical — it is imposed on its subjects from above — while international law between states is coordinative, resting on the agreement of the orders it binds. That contrast returns in every chapter on treaties, peace settlements and international organizations.

cards.q: What is the structural difference between state law and international law in this diagram?
cards.a: State law works downwards within one order — it is imposed on its subjects. International law works sideways between legal orders of equal standing and rests on their agreement, which is why it governs relations between states rather than inside them.

19.title: Europe
19.text: A map opens the series on the words the course uses without defining them — Europe, emperor, Austria. Each turns out to have several meanings, and the exam likes exactly those words.

20.title: Europe: membership before March 2022
20.text: The map shows membership status before March 2022 — that is, with Russia still a member of the Council of Europe. 'Europe' here is not a geographical fact but an institutional membership, and the boundary moves when the institutions move.

21.title: Europe: membership since March 2022
21.text: The same map after March 2022, when Russia ceased to be a member of the Council of Europe following the invasion of Ukraine. Two slides, two maps, one lesson: what counts as 'Europe' is decided by institutions and can change within a month.

cards.q: Why does the lecture show two maps of 'Europe', before and since March 2022?
cards.a: To show that Europe in this course is an institutional and legal concept, not a geographical constant: Russia's membership ended in March 2022, and the map of 'Europe' changed with it.

22.title: Emperor: the Austrian imperial crown
22.text: The Austrian imperial crown with orb and sceptre in the Vienna Imperial Treasury opens the second contested word: emperor.

23.title: The Roman Empire, divided 395
23.text: The map of the division of 395 AD sets up the genealogy of the imperial title on the next slide.

24.title: The imperial title: the first branching
24.text: The line starts with the Roman Emperor of the first to fourth centuries AD. In 395 it divides: a Western Emperor, who lasts until 476, and an Eastern Emperor. From the East the Byzantine Emperor continues until 1453. In the West, after the gap, the title is revived — the Roman-German Emperor, dated 800/962 to 1806. The two dates are both real: 800 is Charlemagne's coronation, 962 that of Otto I, and which one you take as the beginning depends on whether you count the Frankish or the German line.

terms.def: The revived western imperial title, 800/962–1806 — from Charlemagne's or Otto I's coronation to the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire.

cards.q: Trace the imperial title from the Roman Emperor to 1806.
cards.a: Roman Emperor (1st–4th c. AD) → divided in 395 into a Western Emperor (to 476) and an Eastern Emperor → the Eastern line continues as Byzantine Emperor until 1453; in the West the title is revived as the Roman-German Emperor, 800/962 to 1806.

cards.q: Why are the Roman-German Emperors dated '800/962' with two dates?
cards.a: 800 is Charlemagne's imperial coronation, 962 that of Otto I. Which counts as the start depends on whether the Frankish revival or the German line is taken as the beginning of the continuous title.

25.title: Europe around 1000
25.text: The map of Europe around 1000 gives the setting for the eastern continuation of the imperial idea.

26.title: The imperial title: eastern claimants
26.text: The diagram grows two more branches. The Russian Emperor, 1478–1917: after Constantinople fell in 1453 the claim to the Byzantine succession moved to Moscow — the ruler took the title tsar, itself derived from Caesar, and Moscow was styled the THIRD ROME, after Rome and Constantinople. The Turkish Sultan, until 1922, is set on the same line because the Ottoman ruler held Constantinople and with it a claim of his own to the Roman succession.

terms.def: The claim that after Rome and Constantinople the imperial and Orthodox succession passed to Moscow. It underpins the Russian imperial title from 1478 and the word tsar (from Caesar).

cards.q: Why is Moscow called the 'Third Rome'?
cards.a: Because after the fall of Constantinople in 1453 — the second Rome — Moscow claimed the succession to the Byzantine empire and to Orthodox Christianity. The ruler's title tsar derives from Caesar, and the Russian imperial title is dated from 1478 to 1917.

27.title: The coronation of Napoleon I (1804)
27.text: Jacques-Louis David's Le Sacre de Napoléon (1806/07) marks the moment the imperial title is taken outside the old line altogether.

28.title: The imperial title: the modern branches
28.text: The final layer of the diagram. Emperor of the French, 1804–1815 and again 1852–1870; German Kaiser, 1871–1918; Emperor of Austria, 1804–1918 — that last one created in the same year as Napoleon's, and for the same reason: with a French emperor in the field, the Habsburg ruler needed a title of equal rank independent of the old Roman-German crown, which was dissolved two years later in 1806. Beside them the Russian Emperor to 1917 and the Turkish Sultan to 1922. Four of the five imperial titles end within five years of each other, in the First World War and its aftermath.

cards.q: Why was the title 'Emperor of Austria' created in 1804?
cards.a: Because Napoleon had made himself Emperor of the French that year. The Habsburg ruler needed an imperial title of equal rank that did not depend on the Roman-German crown — which was in fact dissolved in 1806.

cards.q: When do the European imperial titles end?
cards.a: Emperor of the French 1870; German Kaiser 1918; Emperor of Austria 1918; Russian Emperor 1917; Turkish Sultan 1922. Four of the five fall within five years, in the First World War and its aftermath.

29.title: Non-European emperors
29.text: Two columns, and the distinction between them is the exam-relevant part. Held EQUAL to European emperors — that is, recognised in their own right: the Negus of Ethiopia (980 BC–1974 AD), the Tennō of Japan (660 BC to the present), the Huángdi of China (221 BC–1912 AD), the Shah-in-Shah of Persia (1501–1979), the Great Mogul of India (1526–1858). Created according to the EUROPEAN MODEL — that is, imperial titles minted by European powers: Emperor of Abyssinia (a title of the Italian king, 1936–1941), Emperor of Mexico (1864–67), Emperor of Brazil (1822–1889), Emperor of India (a title of the British king, 1876–1947).

cards.q: On what basis does the lecture divide non-European imperial titles into two groups?
cards.a: By whether the title stood in its own right and was treated as equal to a European emperor's — Tennō, Huángdi, Negus, Shah-in-Shah, Great Mogul — or was created on the European model by a European power, such as Emperor of India for the British king (1876–1947) or Emperor of Abyssinia for the Italian king (1936–1941).

30.title: 'Austria' has three meanings
30.text: The third contested word, and the one most likely to appear on the exam. First, the ORIGINAL TERRITORIAL meaning: the 'Land' Austria — margraviate, then duchy — divided along the river Enns into the parts above and below it. Second, the DYNASTIC meaning: the Casa de Austria, the House of Habsburg, where 'Austria' names a family, not a place. Third, the TRANSFERRED TERRITORIAL meaning: the Habsburg states as a whole, the 'Herrschaft zu Österreich', where the name of one land comes to stand for everything the dynasty rules.

terms.def: 'Austria' in its dynastic sense: the House of Habsburg as a family, independent of any territory.
'Austria' in its transferred territorial sense: the whole complex of Habsburg lands, named after one of them.

cards.q: What three meanings does the word 'Austria' carry in legal history?
cards.a: The original territorial one — the Land Austria, margraviate then duchy, divided along the Enns; the dynastic one — Casa de Austria, the House of Habsburg; and the transferred territorial one — the Habsburg states taken together, the Herrschaft zu Österreich.

31.title: Personal union
31.text: A personal union means that one and the same person holds several crowns; it does NOT mean that the jointly controlled institutions lose their independence. Each land keeps its own legal order, its own estates and its own law — what they share is the ruler. Remembering this is what keeps the next slide from being read as the founding of a single Habsburg state in 1526.

terms.def: One person holds several crowns while each realm keeps its own institutions and legal order. Only the ruler is shared.

cards.q: What does a personal union change, and what does it leave untouched?
cards.a: It puts several crowns on one head. It leaves the realms' institutions and legal orders independent — they are not merged, they merely share a ruler.

32.title: From personal union towards one state
32.text: 1526/27: the Habsburgs acquire the Bohemian crown, the Crown of Saint Wenceslas, and the Hungarian crown, the Crown of Saint Stephen. For two centuries this remains a personal union. Only through the reforms of Maria Theresa and Joseph II, 1740–1790, do the Habsburg kingdoms and lands merge into one overall state. The two-hundred-year gap between acquiring the crowns and building a state out of them is the point of the slide.

cards.q: When did the Habsburgs acquire the Bohemian and Hungarian crowns, and when did their lands actually become one state?
cards.a: The crowns of Saint Wenceslas (Bohemia) and Saint Stephen (Hungary) came in 1526/27, but that was a personal union. The kingdoms and lands merged into one overall state only through the reforms of Maria Theresa and Joseph II, 1740–1790.

33.text: Three dates carry the constitutional history of the monarchy: 1804, the Austrian Empire is proclaimed; 1867, the Ausgleich turns it into the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy, two states under one ruler; 1918, the monarchy disintegrates.

cards.q: What happened to the Habsburg monarchy in 1804, 1867 and 1918?
cards.a: 1804: the Austrian Empire is proclaimed. 1867: the compromise with Hungary turns it into the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy. 1918: the monarchy disintegrates.

34.title: Austria after 1918
34.text: The name and the form change repeatedly. 1918: 'German Austria'; from 1919 simply 'Austria'. 1918–1933: a democratic republic, the First Republic. 1934–1938: an authoritarian state. 1938–1945: part of Nazi Germany, called the 'Ostmark' and later the 'Alpen- und Donaugaue' — the name Austria is removed altogether. Since 1945: the Republic of Austria, the Second Republic.

cards.q: Name the phases of Austria between 1918 and 1945 and what each was called.
cards.a: 1918 'German Austria', from 1919 'Austria'; 1918–1933 a democratic republic (the First Republic); 1934–1938 an authoritarian state; 1938–1945 part of Nazi Germany as the 'Ostmark', then the 'Alpen- und Donaugaue'; from 1945 the Republic of Austria (Second Republic).

35.title: Method: the historical questions
35.text: The method section opens with Édouard Manet's The Death of Maximilian (1868/69) — the execution of Emperor Maximilian of Mexico. The historian's questions come first: who, where, when, what, why.

36.title: The historical questions alone
36.text: The same five questions without the picture: who, where, when, what, why.

37.title: Method: the legal question added
37.text: On top of the historical questions the legal historian asks one more: was the act lawful — an execution — or unlawful — a murder? The Manet picture is chosen precisely because the answer is not obvious: Maximilian was shot after a court-martial under a Mexican law of 1862, and whether that made it an execution or a killing depends on which legal order you take as authoritative.

cards.q: What question does the legal historian add to the historian's who/where/when/what/why?
cards.a: Whether the act was lawful or unlawful under the law in force at the time — in Manet's picture, whether the death of Maximilian was an execution or a murder.

38.title: The judge and the legal historian
38.text: The central methodological slide, built as a three-point contrast. The JUDGE must (1) treat one concrete legal system as authoritative, (2) assume a fact as certain — the 'formal truth' — and (3) reach a decision, that is, pass judgement. The LEGAL HISTORIAN (1) must take into account the legal ideas of contemporaries rather than pick a system to apply, (2) does not have to assume any fact as completely certain, and (3) reaches conclusions that have no legal effect. All three differences point the same way: the judge is forced to decide and the historian is not, which is exactly what lets the historian leave a question open.

terms.def: The fact a court must treat as established in order to decide, whether or not it corresponds to what happened. The legal historian is not bound to any such assumption.

cards.q: Set out the three differences between the judge and the legal historian.
cards.a: 1) The judge treats one concrete legal system as authoritative; the historian reconstructs the legal ideas of contemporaries. 2) The judge must assume a fact as certain (formal truth); the historian need not treat anything as fully certain. 3) The judge must decide and the judgement has legal effect; the historian's conclusions have none.

cards.q: Why can a legal historian leave a question open where a judge cannot?
cards.a: Because the judge is under a duty to decide, and to decide must fix both an authoritative legal system and a set of facts. The historian's conclusions have no legal effect, so nothing forces a decision and the evidence may be left inconclusive.

39.title: Sources of legal cognition
39.text: How we find out about the law of the past — Rechtserkenntnisquellen, sources of legal cognition. WRITTEN sources: printed, for example the Reichsgesetzblatt für das Kaisertum Österreich; manuscripts, for example medieval law books; and the internet, for example the Austrian legal information system ris.bka.gv.at. OTHER sources: pictures, monuments, buildings, objects, coats of arms; and audiovisual media such as interviews. Keep this slide and the next apart — this one is about how we learn what the law was, the next about what produced the law in the first place.

terms.def: Anything from which we learn what the law of a period was — written (statute collections, manuscripts, databases) or other (images, buildings, objects, coats of arms, recordings). Not the same as a legal source.

cards.q: Which types of source does legal history use to find out about the past, with an example of each?
cards.a: Written sources: printed (the Reichsgesetzblatt), manuscripts (medieval law books), the internet (ris.bka.gv.at). Other sources: images, monuments, buildings, objects and coats of arms, and audiovisual media such as interviews.

40.title: Legal sources
40.text: What produces law — Rechtsquellen, legal sources, four of them. STATUTORY LAW: acts of a legislator such as a parliament, claiming general validity. JUDICIAL LAW: judges do not merely decide the individual case but create precedents binding on other courts. JURISPRUDENTIAL LAW: the opinion of legal scholars is itself a source of law. CUSTOMARY LAW: custom carried by a legal conviction, opinio iuris. Which of the four dominates is one of the questions the whole course turns on — the common law chapter is about judicial law, the ius commune chapter about jurisprudential law.

terms.def: The legal conviction that makes a practice into customary law: the practice is followed because it is held to be legally required, not merely out of habit.
Law whose source is the opinion of legal scholars. Central to the ius commune, where the writings of the doctors carried authority of their own.

cards.q: Name the four legal sources and say what each rests on.
cards.a: Statutory law — acts of a legislator claiming general validity. Judicial law — judges' decisions creating precedents binding on other courts. Jurisprudential law — the opinion of legal scholars as a source in itself. Customary law — custom carried by a legal conviction (opinio iuris).

cards.q: What must be added to a long-standing practice before it counts as customary law?
cards.a: Opinio iuris — the conviction that the practice is legally required. Habit alone, however old, is not law.

cards.q: What is the difference between a source of legal cognition and a legal source?
cards.a: A source of legal cognition is anything we learn the past law FROM — a statute book, a manuscript, a coat of arms, a recording. A legal source is what PRODUCES law: statute, judicial decision, scholarly opinion, custom. The Reichsgesetzblatt is a source of cognition; the act printed in it is statutory law.
